s: Proof became the form of knowledge for the first time, rather than a rule of thumb.
One plane slicing a cone collects the ellipse, the parabola and the hyperbola in a single stroke.
'Transposing' and 'combining' became, for the first time, actions one could write down.
Hindu-Arabic numerals enter Europe, and sequences appear for the first time in recursive form.
Solution by radicals stops at degree four; beyond that, no one advanced for five hundred years.
Algebra and geometry marry: figures and formulas translate into each other, the foundation of this whole map.
A single margin note forced three centuries of algebraic number theory into existence.
Change itself becomes the object, no longer a static quantity.
The dy/dx and integral signs survive to this day, outliving the results themselves.

t: Zeta function and the Basel problem
s: Sum of 1/n^2 = pi^2/6: the sum of reciprocal squares, and a circle appears in the answer.
A degree-n equation has exactly n complex roots, so complex numbers are no longer 'imaginary'.
Any function can be split into a sum of sines, though convergence could not then be pinned down.
First use of partial differential equations to describe a continuous medium; no general solution exists to this day.
Not 'not found yet' but 'does not exist': a proof that, for the first time, denied a possibility.
Whether an equation can be solved becomes a question about the symmetry of a group.
Oriented area itself is treated as a number and made into something computable.
The metric may vary from point to point, so space itself becomes a variable.
The distribution of the primes is pinned to a single critical line, still unproven.
Geometry = transformation group + invariants: nine geometries ordered in one stroke.
Continuity is defined as a cut, and the gaps in the real line are filled.
Rationals can be listed, reals cannot: infinity acquires sizes for the first time.
Quantities unchanged under continuous deformation become a new object of study.
He marked out the century's directions; roughly half were later settled.
A 'function' that is not a function forces distribution theory into being.
Probability becomes a measure: randomness can now be computed rigorously.
'Points' are replaced by prime ideals, so geometry can be done over any ring.
Dimension need not be an integer, and that piece of common sense was knocked down.
Three hundred and fifty-eight years on, modular forms and elliptic curves finish the margin note.
Ricci flow turns a topological problem into geometric evolution.

t: Sexagesimal approximation of the square root of 2
s: Square root of 2 is about 1.41421296, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.
Fractions written as sums of unit fractions, the ancestor of bringing to a common denominator.
The diagonal of a square is incommensurable with its side, so 'all is number' is refuted by its own theorem.

t: Theory of proportion and method of exhaustion
s: 'Arbitrarily small' replaces 'infinitely small': the prehistoric form of the limit.

t: Upper and lower bounds for pi
s: 3.1408 < pi < 3.1429, squeezed out by inscribed and circumscribed polygons.

who: Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art
s: Coefficients laid out with counting rods and then eliminated: the world's earliest elimination method.
'The finer the cut, the less is lost': a complete statement of the idea of a limit.
This fraction pins pi to six decimal places, nearly a millennium ahead of its time.

t: Arithmetic with zero and negative numbers
s: Zero can take part in calculation for the first time, instead of merely meaning 'nothing'.

t: Binomial coefficients arranged in a triangle
s: Binomial coefficients laid out as a triangle, six hundred years before Pascal.
High-degree elimination with four unknowns; the record stood for five hundred years.
Letters stand for knowns and unknowns, so equations can at last be calculated with.
Multiplication becomes addition, and the arithmetic of navigation and astronomy shrinks sharply.
Frequency settles at probability, for the first time in the form of a theorem.
e^(i pi) + 1 = 0: five constants strung together by one formula.
Pi cannot be written as a fraction, and the proof runs through continued fractions.
Congruences and quadratic reciprocity: number theory becomes a system for the first time.
'Approaches indefinitely' becomes epsilon-delta, and calculus no longer rests on intuition.
Through a point off a line, infinitely many parallels: the fifth postulate is not necessary.
To describe rotations in three dimensions, multiplication gives up commutativity for the first time.
A band with only one face, showing that orientability is not a topological necessity.
e is not a root of any equation with integer coefficients.
The impossibility of squaring the circle is thereby proved.
Points, lines and planes need no definition, only the satisfaction of the axioms.
The range of what counts as integrable is widened, and the cracks in the Riemann integral are filled.
Map a disk continuously into itself, and some point always stays fixed.
In any sufficiently strong system there are true propositions that cannot be proved.
'Computable' is defined as what a machine can do.
When no one wants to change strategy unilaterally, the situation comes to rest.
Deterministic equations can still give unpredictable trajectories.
Converting fractions bred errors everywhere, so he wrote decimal fractions as one notation.

t: Geometria indivisibilibus: the method of indivisibles
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Curved figures cannot be measured directly, so he sliced them into infinitely thin pieces.

t: Lectiones Geometricae: a general construction of tangents
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Tangents each had their own trick; he wanted one uniform construction.

t: Treatise of Algebra: negative numbers vindicated
c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: Negatives were dismissed as absurd numbers; he gave them a place on the number line.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Root finding was hopeless, so he first pinned down the stationary point between two roots.

t: Analyse des Infiniment Petits: the first calculus textbook
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Calculus lay scattered in letters, and he turned it into a book one could teach from.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Function values were hard to compute, so he built the whole function from a power series.

c: 初中 无理数与实数
s: A continued fraction expansion forces a contradiction: e cannot be a ratio of two integers.

t: Wave equation for a vibrating string
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: How a string vibrates was unclear, so he wrote down a partial differential equation.

t: Théorie des fonctions analytiques: power series instead of limits
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Limits were unclear, so he simply bypassed them with power series.

t: Planar geometric representation of complex numbers
c: 高中 复数与复平面
s: Imaginary numbers were thought fictitious; he drew them as points in a plane.

t: Rigorous proof of the intermediate value theorem
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: The intermediate value theorem was only geometric intuition, and he wanted a purely analytic proof.

t: Sufficient conditions for Fourier series convergence
c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: What a trigonometric series actually converges to: he gave a criterion one could check.

c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: Quaternions had already lost commutativity; he gave up associativity as well.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Functions were assumed differentiable almost everywhere, and he built the counterexample.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Integrals depend on partitions and sample points; he proved upper and lower sums must converge together.

c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: Were there new number systems after the quaternions? He showed only three remain.

t: Grundlagen der Arithmetik: number reduced to logic
c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: Nobody could say what a number is, so he tried to derive it from logic.

t: Axiom system for the natural numbers
c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: The natural numbers were used on intuition alone; he compressed them into five axioms.

t: Diagonal proof that the reals are uncountable
c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: Can the reals be listed? He answered with a diagonal refutation.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Length fails on bizarre sets, so he first fixed which sets are measurable.

c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: Cantor's sets embraced everything, so he asked about 'the set of all sets'.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Convergence was discussed sequence by sequence, and he wanted an abstract distance.

c: 本科 极限·导数·积分·级数
s: Function spaces each spoke their own language, so he unified complete normed spaces.

t: Forcing: independence of the continuum hypothesis
c: 本科 实数完备与数系结构
s: The continuum hypothesis hung for eighty years; he proved the axioms cannot decide it.
Perspective drawing wants parallels to meet at infinity, which Euclidean geometry cannot hold.
Solving systems in several unknowns needed a formula that decides outright whether a solution exists.
Solving linear systems, he wanted the solution written straight from the coefficient determinant.
Mapmaking raised the question whether curvature can be measured on the surface alone.
Unique factorization fails among cyclotomic integers, so 'ideal factors' had to be supplied.
Computing a composite linear map with one table demanded matrix multiplication.

t: A surface model of hyperbolic geometry
s: Whether non-Euclidean geometry was consistent required a model one could see.

t: Traité des substitutions: group theory systematized
s: Galois's ideas were too scattered; a systematic, teachable group theory was needed.
He wanted integers to count a space's holes, not merely to ask whether it is connected.
Groups exist beyond permutation groups, so a definition from the multiplication table alone was needed.
Invariant theory produced infinitely many generators, and he had to prove finitely many suffice.
Finite group structure is hard to see directly, so he mapped it to matrices and computed.
Formulas in curved space distort under a change of coordinates; a coordinate-free notation was needed.
Are all closed three-manifolds spheres? Homology criteria were no longer enough.
Ideals in rings grew chaotic, so a condition that ascending chains must stop was needed.
Knots take endlessly many shapes, so a computable and reliable invariant was needed.
Why should what differential forms compute equal the homology of a triangulation?
Can an abstract manifold really sit in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space? It needed proof.

who: S. Eilenberg and S. Mac Lane
s: Homology constructions were numerous and alike, and needed a unified structural language.
The number of solutions of equations over finite fields seemed governed by some topological structure.
Spaces that are locally a product but globally twisted needed a unified account.
Local data on a variety does not assemble into the whole, so sheaves were needed to carry it.
Does homeomorphism imply diffeomorphism? The seven-dimensional sphere gave a counterexample.
Why is the analytic index of an elliptic operator always equal to its topological index?
A quantity emerging from von Neumann algebras unexpectedly turns out to distinguish knots.

t: Correspondence on the problem of points
s: A game stopped midway, and how to split the stakes forced probability to be computed from expectation.
Experience at the gaming table arranged into propositions and proofs gave probability its first textbook.
With no root formula available, one can only iterate along the tangent again and again.

t: Normal curve approximating the binomial distribution
s: With many coin tosses the binomial coefficients become unmanageable, so a continuous curve approximates them.
From known results back to causes, a probability formula running from effect to cause was missing.
More observations than unknowns, all contradicting one another, so one minimizes the sum of squared errors.
To turn probability from a gambling trick into a branch of analysis, the central limit theorem took shape.
How large a gap between observed and expected frequencies counts as significant needed a yardstick.
To prove the law of large numbers without independence, he built dependent random sequences.
Brewing tests gave samples too small for the normal approximation, so a small-sample distribution was built.
Simulating waves by difference equations diverges with a wrong step size, so a stability criterion was needed.
Allocating resources optimally under linear constraints lacked an algorithm that could actually compute.
To measure how much information a message carries, uncertainty was written as entropy.
Gun control, nerves and machines all regulate by feedback and needed one shared language.
Measurements carry noise and models are inaccurate, so how to fuse them into an optimal estimate?
An N-point transform takes N^2 operations; splitting it in half brings it down to N log N.
Many problems look unrelated yet are equally hard, so one 'hardest' benchmark was needed.
Every machine had its own floating-point format, so results changed when you changed machines.
